9 Best Things to Do in Marrakesh 🕌✨ 1) Stay in a Riad 🛏️  feel the authentic Moroccan vibe, from the mosaic tiles to the whisper-quiet courtyards. Riads offer privacy, fewer crowds, and a home-away-from-home feel with traditional decor, often a peaceful rooftop terrace, and staff who treat you like family. Perfect for a truly Moroccan experience without the hotel hustle. 2) Best Coffee at Bacha Coffee ☕️✨ (Location: https://goo.gl/maps/6u3Xx9J9xqv1w9Qw7) Silky espresso, perfectly balanced blends, and a chic, relaxed atmosphere. Great latte art, friendly baristas, and a bright, stylish space to post your vibes. Pro tip: try their signature crush coffee and pastry pairing. 3) Explore the Souks 🧿🌀 Fun tip: haggle with a smile, never agree to the first price! Make it a playful game, sample spices, and test your bargaining skills. Lose yourself in ribbons of color, leather, pottery, and lamps. The thrill of the find is half the fun! 4) Visit Ben Youssef Madrasa 🕌 A jaw-dropping historic site with intricate tilework, carved wood, and serene courtyards. It’s a perfect spot for photos that scream old-world Marrakech charm. 5) Jardin Majorelle 🌿💙 iconic cobalt-blue paths, lush botanical displays, and a peaceful escape from the market buzz. A must-see for color lovers and plant enthusiasts, plus it’s connected to the Yves Saint Laurent legacy. 6) Ourika Valley Day Trip 🚙🌄 about 1 hour from central Marrakech (depending on traffic). What to expect: stunning valley scenery, Berber villages, waterfalls, and a cooler climate. A refreshing break from the medina with photo-worthy viewpoints. 7) Agafay Desert Experience 🐫🏜️ Highlights: camel ride under the open sky, squad  bike moments, and magical desert views. Luxe touch: stay at a desert camp with plush lounges, gourmet meals, and starlit dinners. Perfect for a memorable  outing. 8) Dinner at La Trattoria 🍝🇮🇹  warm, cozy ambiance with authentic Italian flavors in Marrakech. Great for a relaxed evening, fresh pastas, and a lively dining vibe after a day of exploration. 9) Jemaa el-Fnaa - The Heart of Marrakech 🎭💃 Do it for the vibes: bustling square, street performances, snake charmers, and a feast for the senses. Pro tip: bring some cash for photos with performers and for quick bites. Best times: late afternoon into evening when the energy peaks. #Marrakesh #Morocco #TravelTikTok #Riads #Souks

Before giving your opinion about Morocco, you should obviously do a little research first. Step one: open a book about Moroccan history. Yes, an actual book with pages, because apparently watching a few TikToks is not enough to become an expert on an entire country. Start by learning about the Amazigh people, whose presence in North Africa goes back thousands of years. Learn about the different Amazigh communities in Morocco, their historical regions, languages, cultures, and traditions. You can look into groups such as the Rifains in the Rif, the Chleuhs in the Souss and southern regions, Amazigh communities of the Middle Atlas, and many others throughout the country. Because, surprisingly, “Amazigh” does not describe one single identical population living in one exact place. Then study Moroccan history before the Arab and Islamic periods: ancient North African populations, Phoenician and Carthaginian influences, the Roman period, and the different dynasties and political changes that shaped Morocco over time. After that, learn about the spread of Arabic language and culture, as well as the migrations, exchanges, and mixing of populations that happened throughout North African history. Then comes everyone’s favorite part: genetics. This is where you should actually read scientific studies instead of looking at one DNA chart on TikTok and suddenly deciding that you have discovered the complete genetic history of an entire population. Moroccan populations have a complex genetic history, with a major ancient North African component alongside influences from different populations that moved through and interacted with North Africa throughout history. Results can also vary between regions and populations, so maybe don’t take one study about one specific group and use it as the universal answer for every Moroccan. You should also learn the difference between ancestry, culture, language, identity, and genetics, because they are not the same thing. Speaking Arabic does not automatically mean having exactly the same genetic ancestry as every other Arabic-speaking person, just as being Amazigh does not mean belonging to one genetically identical population. Human history is, unfortunately for anyone looking for an easy answer, a little more complicated than a “choose your ethnicity” quiz. Then research Amazigh languages in Morocco, their history and official status, as well as the cultural diversity between different Moroccan regions. Learn how Amazigh, Arab, Moroccan, regional, and family identities can sometimes overlap rather than simply cancel each other out. Finally, after studying all of that, you might actually be ready to talk about Morocco without reducing thousands of years of history to two sentences you found online. If you genuinely want to understand Moroccan origins, you have to look at history, archaeology, languages, migrations, culture, and genetics together. There you go. You can officially begin your studies on Morocco now. Good luck with the curriculum. It’s slightly more complicated than expected. #morocco#aespa#ningning#ⵣ🇲🇦 #aespa

🌴ⵣ AGADIR – THE HEART OF AMAZIGH CULTURE 🇲🇦 Did you know that Agadir is located in the Souss region, one of the most important Amazigh-speaking areas in Morocco? Here are a few things you should know: ⵣ Language: The main Amazigh language spoken in Agadir and the surrounding Souss region is Tashelhit (Tachelhit), one of Morocco’s major Amazigh varieties. ⵣ Heritage: Amazigh traditions are deeply rooted in the region, from traditional clothing and silver jewellery to music, poetry and dance. ⵣ Culture: Ahwach, traditional collective singing and dancing, is an important part of Souss cultural heritage. ⵣ Argan: The Souss region is famous for argan trees and the traditional knowledge of producing argan oil. ⵣ History: Agadir was rebuilt after the devastating earthquake of 1960, but its Amazigh cultural roots remain an essential part of its identity. And here’s something interesting: Tashelhit is the most widely spoken Amazigh language in Morocco. The Souss-Massa region has a particularly high concentration of its speakers. Agadir isn’t just beaches, sunshine and tourism. It’s a city where Amazigh identity, language and traditions are part of everyday life. ⵣ Proud of our roots. Proud of our language. Proud to be Amazigh. #Agadir #Amazigh #morocco #north_african_berbers🇩🇿🇲🇦🇹🇳🇱🇾🇲🇷 #edit
